value: Problem: as companies grow, developers wait for infrastructure tickets, platform teams build brittle internal portals, and security and finance cannot see what was shipped or who paid for it; AI coding agents now multiply the volume of code and the risk. Logic: nullplatform provides the platform as a product, extensible to a mature organisation's own rules, so large companies avoid the cost of building and maintaining an internal platform and get a control point for human and AI-generated code. Its sales argument is a measurable saving (clients report about 30% lower infrastructure and operating cost, a company claim) and speed. Why now: AI agents make governed deployment a board-level topic, cloud costs are under scrutiny, and the founders' team has built such a platform at scale. Market: we found no readable independent market-size report. Our bottom-up estimate, labelled assumption: 500 to 1,500 large and mid-sized enterprises in Latin America and the Spanish-speaking market have 300 or more engineers and a platform-engineering need; at US$150,000 to US$500,000 of annual contract value that is roughly US$75 million to US$750 million a year in the region, with a much larger United States market; the company claims 10,000 engineers served, which at an assumed US$300 per engineer per month would be about US$36 million of annual value, so we regard it as a small share of the regional pool. What is different: leadership that built Mercado Libre's platform, a vendor-independent model that extends to legacy and on-premise systems, and an explicit governance layer for AI agents. Competitors named in the press we read: none; from our own knowledge, commercial and open-source internal developer platforms (Backstage-based portals, Humanitec, Port, Cycloid), cloud-provider tools and in-house platforms. value: Alchemy sells an AI-native ERP for accounting and finance to fast-growing technology and service companies, in which agents capture, classify, post and reconcile documents and executives can operate it from Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini.
note: Site read 2026-11-24 (Portuguese and English).

value: Alchemy is a São Paulo company that sells an "AI-native" ERP: an accounting and finance system for fast-growing technology and service companies, typically with R$20 million to R$500 million of revenue, which today run on spreadsheets or an ERP that has not kept up. Its argument is that AI is in the engine rather than bolted on: agents fetch the invoices and payment slips issued against the customer (from e-mail, the national invoice portal and the DDA direct-debit feed), read documents, classify entries, apply the company's own deterministic accounting rules, calculate taxes, post to the ledger, reconcile bank statements, schedule billing, flag errors and keep budget and forecast current. It says more than 90% of reconciliations happen without human intervention, close is continuous (hours, not weeks), and every posted entry is immutable and traceable back to the supplier e-mail that started it. The product has eight modules on one ledger: cash, receivables, payables, purchasing, people (CLT and contractor payroll, ISS withholding, tax credits), FP&A and the accounting core. It supports multi-entity, multi-currency consolidation under Brazilian CPC/IFRS, US GAAP and Mexican NIF, connects to more than 130 financial institutions through Open Finance, bank files, cards and Pix, and works with Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini through MCP, so a CEO can ask an assistant for margin by customer and get the number straight from the ERP under the same permissions. Implementation is promised in a week with no setup fee; pricing is an annual subscription with no per-user charge. Co-founder and CEO Fernando Ribeiro was CFO of the insurtech Pitzi and worked at the hedge fund Bridgewater; co-founder and CTO Willian Menegali leads technology. In Brazil Journal's sponsored launch piece (about September 2026) Ribeiro frames the pain as ERP implementations that take nine months on average (Panorama Consulting) and as customers feeling like hostages, and says the goal is for clients to grow from R$20 million to over R$500 million of revenue with the same three-person finance team. The company says its base already includes customers with operations in Brazil, Mexico and the United States, many migrated from spreadsheets, Omie and TOTVS, and it presents the Brazilian tax reform (two parallel tax regimes until 2032) as the reason to switch now. It compares itself to Rillet, a US AI-native ERP the article says is valued at US$1 billion. It targets CFOs, controllers and heads of finance in technology and services firms and says it is not suited to retail, manufacturing, construction, agriculture or logistics where inventory and fixed assets are central. The careers site says customers run in four countries and that the company is backed by global funds; the founding date, funding rounds and customer names are not public on the pages we read.
note: Pages used: https://usealchemy.io/ and https://usealchemy.io/en/ (product, modules, FAQ, target customers, 2026-11-24); https://braziljournal.com/brands/alchemy-lanca-o-primeiro-erp-ai-native-do-brasil-o-sistema-que-trabalha-nao-so-registra (Brazil Journal "Brands" launch piece, a sponsored "Um conteúdo" article dated "2 months ago" on 2026-11-24, read from a PDF the owner supplied: founders, backgrounds, customers in three countries, tax reform, Rillet); https://carreiras.usealchemy.io/ (four countries, global funds); https://www.linkedin.com/company/alchemy-erp (location, via Linked API search 2026-11-24). Figures and positioning are the company's own.

value: Problem: growing service and technology companies outgrow spreadsheets and entry-level accounting software, but ERPs take nine months to implement on average (Panorama Consulting, quoted in Brazil Journal), turn the CFO into a project manager, and still leave more than half of mid-sized and large firms feeding the ERP manually, with 40% relying only on spreadsheets to consolidate results (survey figures quoted in the same article). Logic: Alchemy rebuilds the ledger around agents that capture, classify, reconcile and post under deterministic rules, so the team reviews exceptions; exposing it to an AI assistant over MCP makes finance queryable by executives. Why now: language models can read invoices and e-mails reliably enough to do clerical work; Brazil's tax reform forces companies to compute taxes in two regimes until 2032, which prompts system reviews; and Open Finance and the national invoice portal give machine-readable data. Market: we found no readable independent market-size report. Our bottom-up estimate, labelled assumption: between 10,000 and 30,000 Brazilian technology and services companies fall in the R$20 million to R$500 million revenue band; at R$120,000 to R$400,000 a year of subscription (our guess, since pricing is not published) that is R$1.2 to R$12 billion, roughly US$0.2 to 2 billion a year, with Mexico and the United States adding more. A strong outcome is 3% to 5% of the Brazilian pool: US$10 to 100 million of revenue. Comparable: Rillet in the United States, which Brazil Journal says is valued at US$1 billion with Sequoia and a16z as investors (a claim in a sponsored piece). What is different: continuous close with immutability and a full audit trail, an assistant interface via MCP, multi-country entities in one ledger, and the no-implementation-fee promise that attacks the main cost of incumbents. Customers have migrated from Omie and TOTVS, which are also the incumbents; Sankhya and Senior are adding AI agents too (named in search results, not read). Fit with Norte (our reading): the first customers are the finance teams of fast-growing start-ups like those in Norte's network, and the CEO's profile (startup CFO plus Bridgewater) is the operator-founder type the Manifesto describes; we could not confirm Norte's participation or funding. Risks: incumbents are shipping similar agents and have distribution; ERP replacement is a slow, high-trust sale; AI accounting errors are costly; and almost nothing is public on revenue, funding or customer names, so this thesis rests on company statements.
note: Market arithmetic is ours: 10,000-30,000 companies x R$120,000-400,000 a year = R$1.2-12 billion, about US$0.2-2 billion at R$5.5 per dollar; 3-5% of the Brazilian pool = US$10-100 million. Nine-month implementation (Panorama Consulting), the manual-ERP survey figures, Rillet at US$1 billion and the tax-reform timeline are quoted in https://braziljournal.com/brands/alchemy-lanca-o-primeiro-erp-ai-native-do-brasil-o-sistema-que-trabalha-nao-so-registra, a sponsored article. value: ZAX is a São Paulo marketplace where small shop owners and resellers buy clothing and accessories at wholesale prices straight from suppliers in the Brás, Bom Retiro and other fashion districts, with freight and payment handled on the platform.
note: Own wording from the site (read 2026-11-24), the Exame and Startupi 2021 articles.

value: ZAX is an online wholesale marketplace for fashion in Brazil. It connects small and mid-sized retailers (clothing shops, resellers, independent sellers) with factories and wholesalers in São Paulo's traditional wholesale districts, the Brás, Bom Retiro and 25 de Março, and, more recently, Fortaleza. The buyer browses a catalogue, compares prices from many suppliers, picks a freight option (or collects at the supplier) and pays in a way that fits their cash flow: up to six card instalments, Pix, bank slip or a boleto with a payment term. The site stresses that there is no minimum order and that more than a thousand suppliers are listed. Before ZAX, shop owners from the interior often took long bus trips to the Brás to restock, ordered on paper or WhatsApp and had little working capital; the founders say wholesale had about 1% e-commerce penetration against about 7% in retail. ZAX started in 2019 as a clothing marketplace for the state of São Paulo and, from 2020, added shoes, electronics, toys, accessories and beauty. It earns from the transactions on the platform and from services around them: in April 2021 it added 30-day working-capital credit and a point-of-sale payment solution through partners, and planned a digital wallet and buy-now-pay-later pilots. It was founded by Bruno Ballardie, who had built and sold the eyewear e-commerce eÓtica, and Fernando Zanatta, a former CTO of Dafiti and technology director at Netshoes, both second-time founders with consumer e-commerce backgrounds who chose to digitise B2B trade. Growth came during the pandemic: suppliers rose from about 100 to about 700 and revenue grew ten times from March 2020; by October 2021 it listed more than 900 sellers, 70,000 items and 50,000 registered shops, with a team of 40 to 65 people. In 2021 it raised R$32 million led by Atlantico to hire, add categories and open other wholesale hubs (Maringá, Brusque, Goiânia, Fortaleza and Santa Cruz do Capibaribe were being studied). The app today also invites consumers to buy at retail or wholesale with factory prices, which suggests the company has widened its audience beyond resellers; no article after 2021 explains how the business has evolved, so its current size is unknown.
note: Draws on https://exame.com/insight/zax-startup-que-digitaliza-o-atacado-do-bras-capta-r-32-milhoes/p/ (origin, GFC and Canary cheques, 900 sellers, expansion cities), https://au.finance.yahoo.com/news/b2b-marketplace-zax-targets-latin-120017237.html (TechCrunch via Yahoo, 5 Oct 2021: 700 suppliers, 10x revenue since March 2020, 65 employees, 1% and 7% penetration, BNPL pilots), https://zaxapp.com.br (current supplier count, payment terms, Fortaleza, read 2026-11-24) and https://apps.apple.com/BR/app/id1464778068 (retail and wholesale wording). Startupi says team of 40, TechCrunch 65; kept both as a range.

value: Problem: Brazil has roughly 1.5 million fashion shops (Exame, 2021, citing R$229 billion a year in sales) and many more independent resellers. They restock in person in a few districts (Brás, Bom Retiro, 25 de Março), travelling for hours, ordering by WhatsApp or paper, paying cash or on short terms and having no way to compare suppliers. Suppliers, for their part, reach only the buyers who show up. Logic: a marketplace that puts hundreds of factories on one catalogue, solves freight and payment, and adds credit works because the supply side is concentrated (a few thousand suppliers in a few streets, so onboarding is tractable) and the demand side is large and fragmented; the 2020 to 2021 pandemic forced shops to buy online and ZAX reported revenue growing ten times and suppliers going from about 100 to 700. Market size: the company's own figure is a B2B market of R$2.4 trillion in 2019 with about 1% online (E-Consulting via Startupi; a company claim and a very broad number, not a market for this product). Our bottom-up estimate, with labelled assumptions: 1.5 million fashion shops with R$229 billion of sales; if goods bought from wholesalers are about half of that (assumption: cost of goods around 50% of sales) the wholesale purchases are about R$115 billion a year; if the online share reached 5% to 10% (assumption; today about 1%) that is R$6 billion to R$11 billion a year; if ZAX held 10% to 20% of that online volume it would move R$0.6 billion to R$2 billion a year, which at an 8% to 15% take rate (assumption) is about R$50 million to R$300 million in revenue, plus credit and payments income. That is a good venture outcome in Brazil, and the model can be copied in other districts and Latin American countries, as Atlantico's partner said. What is different: a team of second-time founders from large consumer e-commerce (Dafiti, Netshoes, Buscapé, eÓtica), a focus on the Brás wholesale culture instead of a generic B2B catalogue, and payment terms and credit built around the shop owner's cash flow. We read no page on rivals or comparables, so none is assessed here. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does, and helps by connecting people and bringing top funds onto the cap table; ZAX's founders match the operator profile, and a follower role at an early stage (the 2019 and 2020 rounds were led by GFC and Canary) fits that approach. This is our reading, not a Norte statement. Risks: marketplaces leak, since a supplier and buyer who have met can trade off the platform; general marketplaces and WhatsApp commerce can compete for the same shop owners (our assumption, no page read); credit adds default risk; and we found no news after 2021, no later round and no revenue figure, so traction after the pandemic is unproven.

Arithmetic: 229bn x 50% = 114.5bn; x 5%-10% = 5.7-11.5bn; x 10%-20% = 0.57-2.3bn; x 8%-15% = 46m-345m (rounded in the text). The 50% cost of goods, 5-10% online share, 10-20% ZAX share and 8-15% take rate are our assumptions. Norte lens from https://www.norte.ventures/ read 2026-11-24. Confidence low: no independent market report read and no post-2021 traction.

value: Yuno is a payments orchestration platform: one API that lets large merchants, banks and wallets accept payments, payouts, fraud checks and stablecoins across more than 1,000 payment methods in 190+ countries, with smart routing and AI agents to raise approval rates.
note: Own wording from the company homepage and the Series B press release (read 2026-11-24).

value: Yuno is a global payments orchestration company founded by two former Rappi executives. Large online merchants usually work with half a dozen payment providers, acquirers and fraud tools, each with its own integration, local methods and failure modes. Yuno puts them behind one API and one dashboard: it routes each transaction to the provider most likely to approve it at the lowest cost, retries failures, offers one-click checkout, handles pay-ins, payouts, subscriptions, reconciliation, fraud prevention, KYC and KYB, and stablecoins, and now sells itself as an AI-native system whose specialised agents recover failed payments and tune routing. It says it connects to more than 1,000 payment methods and 460 integrations in 190+ countries, and that in a year it recovered over US$5 billion of failed volume, lifted authorisation rates by about 5 percent and saved merchants more than US$500 million in processing cost. Its revenue comes from the payment volume that merchants run through it, plus white-label deals with banks and processors such as dLocal and Mexico's Prosa. The idea came from Juan Pablo Ortega, who helped start Rappi and built its payments and fraud teams and RappiBank, and Julián Núñez, who created Rappi's one-click checkout and led its e-commerce unit; they teamed up in 2021 and formally founded Yuno in January 2022. After a first cheque from Andreessen Horowitz it closed a US$10 million seed in March 2022, co-led by Kaszek and Monashees, with 40 employees and Rappi as first customer; the product launched in October 2022 focused on Mexico, Brazil and Colombia. In March 2024 it raised a US$25 million Series A at a reported US$150 million valuation with DST Global Partners, a16z, Tiger Global, Kaszek and Monashees, then had enterprise customers such as McDonald's, Avianca and inDrive in 50 countries and set out to expand to Europe, Asia and Africa. It opened offices on five continents (16 listed on its site), a Gulf regional hub in Doha, and in April 2026 its Saudi unit received a Payment Technical Service Provider licence from the Saudi Central Bank. In August 2026 it raised a US$45 million Series B led by Global PayTech Ventures to reach profitability, add in-person payments and agentic commerce and grow in the United States; it says it is on track to process US$100 billion in annual volume within 12 months, for customers that now include McDonald's, NetEase Games, GoFundMe, inDrive, Rappi and Uber. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, November 2026): Yuno is selling local payment methods through one integration, with a direct Nequi connection in Colombia, while it hires for partnerships in LATAM, Brazil, North America and Mexico, and for engineering, incident and risk leadership, including remote roles in Europe.
note: Draws on https://y.uno/newsroom/yuno-series-b (Series B, volumes, customers, licence, partners), https://techcrunch.com/2022/03/10/with-founders-hailing-from-colombian-unicorn-rappi-startup-yuno-raises-10m-from-a16z-and-latam-vcs and https://prnewswire.com/news-releases/yuno-raises-us10m-seed-round-to-solve-online-payments-in-latin-america-301499891.html (founders, seed, 40 employees, Rappi, Mexico-Brazil-Colombia focus, founded January 2022), https://techcrunch.com/?p=2673996 (product launch October 2022, US$150M valuation, 150 integrations, enterprise focus), https://www.malaymail.com/news/money/mediaoutreach/2024/03/06/yuno-secures-us25m-planning-europe-asia-expansion/282508 (Series A investors, 50 countries, expansion plans), https://www.y.uno/en/about (offices, timeline) and https://y.uno (product, AI agents, 1,000+ methods). Current state added from LinkedIn posts found by Linked API search-posts on 2026-11-24 (https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:ugcPost:7525546000137273347).

value: Problem: a global merchant (an airline, a food chain, a game publisher) must accept payments in many countries through many acquirers, wallets, bank-transfer schemes and cash vouchers, each with its own integration, approval rates, fees and fraud rules; in Latin America, where cards are a minority of payments and local methods such as Pix, OXXO and PSE matter, the fragmentation is worst. Logic: an orchestration layer lets the merchant add a market or a provider in days, route to the best acquirer per transaction, retry failures and consolidate reporting; every point of approval rate is revenue the merchant already earned, so the value is easy to measure (Yuno claims US$5 billion of recovered volume and US$500 million of cost saved in a year), and the volume is recurring. Why now: cross-border and local-method commerce keeps growing, merchants had already built the multi-provider mess, and enterprise buyers began issuing RFPs just for orchestration (TechCrunch, 2024). Market size: published research puts the software market for payment orchestration platforms at about US$2.7 billion in 2025 growing to about US$7.3 billion in 2031 (Mordor Intelligence; other firms range from US$1.9 billion to US$9 billion, so this is a rough order of magnitude), and TechCrunch cited about US$7 billion by 2032. A bottom-up view is better suited to a volume business: Yuno says it is on track to process US$100 billion a year; at an assumed net take rate of 0.1% to 0.2% of volume (our assumption, between a pure software fee and a processor's margin) that is US$100 million to US$200 million of revenue a year, and the share of the orchestration market that implies is large, which suggests either that the research figures understate volume-based pricing or that the take rate is lower. A strong outcome is a leading enterprise orchestrator in emerging markets, comparable to dLocal (a listed cross-border processor and a Yuno partner, per the Series B release). What is different: enterprise focus when many rivals (Gr4vy, Plug, Revio) serve SMBs; over 460 integrations built in emerging markets; founders who ran the problem at Rappi across nine countries; and an AI-agent layer on top of the routing data. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and that it brings top funds and angels onto the cap table; Yuno's seed was co-led by Kaszek and Monashees with a16z, so a Norte role would be as a follower or angel-type connector; Norte's participation is not stated in any source we read. This is our reading, not Norte's. Risks: TechCrunch names Gr4vy, Plug, Revio and Simetrik as rivals and large payment processors may add orchestration features (our assumption), and orchestration can be commoditised, enterprise sales cycles are long, and take rate and gross margin are undisclosed.

value: Baze offers the "Linha Baze", a revolving credit line in Brazil secured by the customer's property or vehicle: opened once, reused as it is repaid, at rates from CDI plus 0.7% a month, entirely through an app.
note: Own wording from the company site (read 2026-11-24).

value: Baze is a São Paulo fintech that sells what it calls the first "Linha Patrimonial" in Brazil: a revolving credit line backed by a property or vehicle that the customer already owns, fully paid or with a low balance. The pitch is that wealth tied up in a house or a car should work as financial infrastructure, as home-equity credit does in the United States (the site cites about US$350 billion outstanding there against less than 1% of Brazilian families with a paid-off property having anything similar). Unlike a personal loan (which the site prices at 5% to 15% a month) or a traditional home-equity loan (1.5% to 3% a month, weeks to release, a new contract for each use), the Linha Baze is opened once, with no end date: the customer signs in the app, connects Open Finance data, receives a "Carta Baze" stating limit, rate and terms, and Baze handles the registry, notary and formalisation. Each withdrawal is repaid in instalments the customer chooses, and the limit regenerates as it is paid down, which the company describes as an "adaptive intelligence" that adjusts the line to the customer's income and cash flow. Pricing is post-fixed, from CDI plus 0.7% a month. Typical uses on the site are renovations, working capital for a small business, replacing expensive card or overdraft debt, buying a second property, medical bills, education and divorce settlements. Baze also builds a channel of 30 hand-picked "founding partners" (wealth advisers, accountants and lawyers, family offices, real-estate agents and architects, and credit correspondents), who earn a commission on every withdrawal their client makes. The company was registered in December 2024 and a US limited liability company joined as a partner in October 2025; a Baze FIDC (a receivables fund) is registered with the CVM, administered by Vórtx and managed by Harbour Capital, and still pre-operational in the regulator's data, which suggests the credit is meant to be funded through a fund structure. The site mentions "investors, technology partners and custody regulated by the Central Bank" but names none. We found no press coverage, no named founders in public text and no round, so the company is very young and its size is unknown.

value: Problem: Brazilian families and small-business owners with a paid-off property or car sit on assets but borrow with personal loans, overdrafts and cards at 5% a month or more because home-equity loans are slow, notary-heavy and re-done for each use. Logic: since 1 July 2025 the "Marco das Garantias" lets the same property back several credit operations, which is what makes a reusable line over one collateral possible, and Open Finance data lets a lender size the limit and the risk without paper; a revolving product over secured collateral can charge much less than unsecured credit and still earn a spread over the CDI. Market size: Abecip data cited by Portas show home-equity originations of R$3.17 billion in the first quarter of 2026, up 25.8% on a year earlier and the highest first quarter since the series began in 2018; annualised that is about R$12 billion to R$13 billion, tiny compared with the stock of residential property. If the segment kept growing 25% a year for four years it would reach about R$31 billion a year by 2030 (our extrapolation); a company that took 3% to 5% of that would originate about R$0.9 billion to R$1.6 billion a year. Because a revolving line is reused, balances and revenue per client could exceed a one-shot loan, though credit risk and funding cost decide the economics. What is different: the product framing (a permanent, regenerating line instead of a loan), app-only onboarding with Open Finance, a curated advisory channel paid per withdrawal, and a planned fund structure for funding. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does, and brings top funds and angels onto cap tables and generates revenue from day zero; a secured-credit fintech needs funding partners and distribution, which is where a network helps. This is our reading, not a Norte statement, and we do not know the founders' backgrounds. Risks: credit and collateral risk if the cycle turns, dependence on a funding vehicle that is still pre-operational, a regulated activity (the company is a financial-institution correspondent per its registry), incumbent banks and home-equity lenders with cheaper funding, and no public traction data. Evidence is thin: one company site, a registry, a fund page and a market article.

value: Pomelo is an Argentine payments-infrastructure company that lets banks, fintechs and large companies issue and process prepaid, debit and credit cards across Latin America through one API, including its own network licences (BIN sponsorship).
note: Own wording from the company site and the Bloomberg Línea (Jan 2026) and TechCrunch (2024) articles.

value: Pomelo is a Buenos Aires company that sells the plumbing behind card programmes in Latin America. A fintech, bank or global company that wants to launch prepaid, debit, credit or corporate cards (physical, virtual or digital) would normally spend 12 to 18 months and repeat the process in each country; Pomelo offers a modular, API-first platform that handles issuing, tokenisation, printing and logistics, real-time transaction processing, a credit core, wallet migration and fraud prevention, and can act as the "BIN sponsor" so that smaller clients launch under Pomelo's Visa and Mastercard licences without building the regulatory and compliance layer themselves. Its use cases range from replacing a traditional processor and corporate cards to crypto wallets, remittances, instant funding, stablecoin payments and single-use cards for travel agencies and agentic payments. It earns from processing and issuing fees on the volume that runs through the platform. The company was started in early 2021 by three executives: Gastón Irigoyen, a third-time founder with two exits (one to TripAdvisor), early Google Latin America employee and former CEO of Naranja X, Argentina's largest neobank; Juan Fantoni, former fintech director at Mastercard; and Hernán Corral, former product chief of Naranja X and head of digital accounts and cards at Mercado Pago. It raised a US$9 million seed in May 2021 when it was three months old and had no product, a US$35 million Series A led by Tiger Global in October 2021 (when it had 100 employees), a US$15 million extension in August 2022 that added Bill Maris's Section 32 and took it to Colombia and Peru, a US$40 million Series B led by Kaszek in January 2024 and a US$55 million Series C co-led by Kaszek and Insight Partners in January 2026. Its first customer went live in January 2022 with prepaid cards in Argentina; by 2024 it served more than 100 corporate clients (Rappi, Bitso, Stori, Nomad, PayJoy, Ripio, AstroPay) in Argentina, Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Peru, revenue had tripled in 2023, payments volume had grown seven times and it could process 55 million transactions a day. By January 2026 it had over 150 clients including BBVA, Santander and Bancolombia, Binance and Western Union, with Mexico and Brazil as its largest markets; the Series C funds a global stablecoin-denominated credit card (initially on Circle's USDC), real-time and agentic payments, and expansion beyond Latin America. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, November 2026): after the US$55 million Series C, Pomelo has hired a new CFO and is pushing a global card-issuing offer and cross-border payments, including stablecoins and other digital assets, while adding fintech partners such as Racional in Chile.

value: Problem: in Latin America issuing cards is slow and fragmented: each country needs its own processor, network licences and compliance, so a fintech or a bank takes 12 to 18 months to launch a card (company, 2021) and must repeat it for each market. Logic: cards are still the dominant digital payment in the region, and every new fintech, neobank, remittance app or loyalty programme needs an issuer-processor; a single modern, API-first processor with network licences lets clients launch in weeks and expand country by country, and processing revenue grows with client volume without the platform's cost growing at the same rate. Why now: the neobank and embedded-finance wave, the move of traditional banks (BBVA, Santander, Bancolombia are now customers per Bloomberg Línea) away from legacy processors, and new demand for stablecoin cards and agentic payments. Market size: the company said in 2021 that cards in the region carry about US$900 billion of payments a year, 95% processed by local incumbents (company claim, via TechCrunch). Our estimate of the processing and issuing pool: if issuer-processing and BIN-sponsorship take 0.05% to 0.2% of volume (our assumption), the pool is about US$0.45 billion to US$1.8 billion a year at 2021 volumes, and larger as card volume grows; a leader that held 10% to 20% would earn about US$45 million to US$360 million a year, with more from the credit core and the global stablecoin card. Reported traction is consistent: revenue tripled in 2023 and was expected to double again in 2024, and 150+ clients by 2026. What is different: it was built cloud-native after the incumbents, pursues both fintechs and banks, offers BIN sponsorship that lowers the barrier for small clients, and covers six countries on one platform. Comparables the company itself cites are Galileo, Marqeta and Stripe in the United States. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does; Pomelo's founders (ex-Naranja X, Mastercard, Mercado Pago) and its round leaders (Index, monashees, Tiger, Kaszek) suggest Norte would have been a small follower connecting the company with operators and funds; no source we read names Norte. This is our reading. Risks: incumbent processors and other fintech infrastructure (the company names Galileo and Marqeta as models, not rivals) can compete on price; revenue concentrates in a few large clients; client fintechs are exposed to credit and rate cycles; Argentina's macroeconomic and currency risk affects the home base; and the stablecoin card faces regulatory uncertainty.

value: Lemon connects clean-energy plants (mostly solar) to small businesses, condominiums and households in Brazil: customers receive energy credits on their grid bill, save on electricity and need no installation or upfront cost.
note: Own wording from the company site (read 2026-11-24), Kaszek and Startups.com.br.

value: Lemon Energia is a Brazilian energy-tech company that sells distributed-generation solar energy as a subscription. Remote plants, owned by third-party generators, feed energy into the local distribution network; this produces credits that are discounted from the electricity bill of Lemon's customers, who pay Lemon instead (and a residual conventional charge to the utility) and usually save 10% to 20%. Customers need no panels, works or upfront payment, sign up online and manage billing in an app with Pix or boleto payment; they can cancel at any time. On the other side, generators that would otherwise sell wholesale reach the retail market and, per Kaszek, can nearly double their earnings, while Lemon takes over billing, collection and energy management. It earns a fee charged to the generators. The target started as small and mid-sized businesses (bars, restaurants, groceries, supermarkets, laundries spending R$500 to R$8,000 a month on power), and the site now also addresses homes, companies and condominiums. The founders are Rafael Vignoli (CEO), Luciano Pereira (CTO) and Rafael Mezzomo, with Ariel Amar (CFO) named as a co-founder in 2020 and 2022 coverage. It started in 2019 with early customers such as the Oyo hotel chain; when the pandemic hit that concentration, it pivoted to bars and restaurants, piloted with 200 establishments with the utility Cemig in Minas Gerais and in October 2020 took an investment from Ambev's corporate venture arm Z-Tech, which led to a role in Ambev's and Budweiser's "Energy Collective" to bring clean energy to up to 250,000 bars by 2025. After a R$60 million Series A in June 2022 led by Kaszek (with Lowercarbon Capital, its first investment in Brazil), it grew from 3,000 clients and 6 states to about 10,000 clients in 2024 and, by July 2026, 40,000 clients, more than 250 connected plants (against fewer than 50 in 2022), over ten states and more than 15 utilities. A recent growth channel is taking over the customer portfolios of generators that no longer want to run retail, and it is considering acquisitions to consolidate the sector. Next it plans a residential product and entry into Brazil's "free market" for energy, which opens to low-voltage commercial users in November 2027 and to households in November 2028 and would let it serve large cities such as São Paulo and Rio, where distributed generation is limited by the rule that plant and consumer must be in the same utility area. Lemon won gold at the 2026 Energy Summit Awards in sustainability. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, 2026): the founder Rafael Vignoli still leads the company, and in March 2026 it was picked for KPMG's Emerging Giants list of scale-ups, with Norte confirming it as a portfolio company.

value: Problem: Brazil has more than 80 million electricity consumer units (Lemon's CEO, 2022) that are bill payers, not customers: they pay high tariffs, have no choice of supplier and, for small businesses and renters, cannot install solar because of upfront cost, space or ownership. Hydro supplies about two thirds of power and Kaszek notes that droughts push prices up and solar is under 2% of the mix. Logic: distributed generation rules let a consumer receive credits from a plant in the same utility area, so a software company that signs up many small consumers, matches them to plants and handles billing creates savings for the customer and better prices for the generator, with a low acquisition cost through partners; Lemon says its unit economics are good and growth came at low acquisition cost. Why now: new distributed-generation regulation, the ESG push, and the planned opening of the free energy market (November 2027 for low-voltage commercial users, November 2028 for households), which would let Lemon serve São Paulo and Rio. Market size: no independent figure was read, so we estimate bottom-up with labelled assumptions: 80 million consumer units x an assumed average bill of R$1,800 a year (R$150 a month) is about R$144 billion a year of retail electricity bills; if 3% to 5% were served through subscription-type clean energy that is R$4 billion to R$7 billion a year billed, and at an assumed 10% to 15% gross take on billings Lemon's pool is R$0.4 billion to R$1 billion in revenue, of which a leader could hold a large share. Traction fits: 40,000 clients and 250 plants in 2026, up from 10,000 in 2022. What is different: a technology and customer-experience focus in a market of analog utilities and small generators (CTO's own words in 2022), customer acquisition through partners (such as Ambev), and a portfolio-takeover channel that consolidates distressed generators. Competitors named in the press: Sunne (similar model) and, with a financing model, Meu Financiamento Solar, Solfácil and Nextron. Fit with Norte: a 2022 Startups.com.br article lists Norte among Lemon's investors before the Series A; the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and generates revenue from day zero by connecting people, which fits an Ambev distribution partnership; this is our reading. Risks: regulation (the distributed-generation framework, utility and tariff rules) changes the economics; generator and customer credit risk; thin take rates; the free market opening also invites bigger energy traders; and the company said in 2023 it did not expect break-even soon.

value: Morado is a Colombian fintech that sells beauty products and credit to hair salons, barbershops and nail studios, financing their supplier purchases at 30, 60 or 90 days through an app and WhatsApp.
note: Own wording from the company site, Latamlist (Jan 2025) and Descubre.vc.

value: Morado is a Bogotá-based company that started in 2022 as an online "everything store" for beauty businesses and has become a credit provider for them. Its founder, Ángela Acosta, spent about eight years at Rappi, from intern to vice president, working on grocery and on the fintech side (Rappi Pay and RappiBank), and in 2021 resigned to build something for the beauty industry; she even took a manicurist course to talk with women who ran salons and heard that the lack of capital was their main obstacle. The first version was a vertical marketplace and logistics business: more than 6,500 products at launch (20,000 by early 2023), no minimum order, same-day or next-day delivery from warehouses in Barranquilla and Bogotá, national coverage in Colombia within 30 days and more than 60 employees, most of them women. She described 700,000 beauty salons in Latin America whose supply chain had not changed in 40 years, 85% of them without any digital tool. The business then moved toward finance: salons order supplies and Morado funds the purchase for 30, 60 or 90 days, assessing risk with traditional data plus non-financial signals such as headcount, location, inventory and client appointments, starting with small loans (about US$820 on average) and raising limits as clients repay. According to Morado, over 72% of its borrowers had their first credit with it and more than half had no bank account. The company site says 28,000 women-led businesses have grown with it, US$12 million in sales and that 64% of the businesses it finances never had credit; it is an award winner of the IDB Lab WeXchange programme and of Forbes Colombia's "30 promesas" of 2023, and its 2024 impact report is published. Morado raised a US$5 million pre-seed in April 2022 led by Tiger Global and H20 Capital with a16z (where it joined the START programme), QED, Latitud, Village Global and Rappi founders as angels. The site later announces a new round of equity and debt without giving date or size. The stated plans were to expand to Mexico, which we found no evidence of, and to grow from 30,000 to a million businesses.
note: Draws on https://forbes.co/2022/04/20/emprendedores/la-exrappi-que-esta-construyendo-un-amazon-para-peluquerias/ (Forbes Colombia, 20 Apr 2022: origin, warehouses, round), https://techcrunch.com/?p=2302919 (TechCrunch, 20 Apr 2022: market, a16z START, Mexico plan), https://forbes.co/30-promesas-2023/morado (2023 traction), https://latamlist.com/?p=16175 (Latamlist, 14 Jan 2025: credit model, US$820, 72%), https://moradocolombia.com/sobre-morado (28,000 businesses, US$12M, 64%, new round of equity and debt) and https://www.descubre.vc/e/morado (Descubre.vc profile). Company-reported figures are not independently verified; the 1 million community figure on the about page is not used.

value: Problem: Latin America has about 700,000 beauty salons (the founder's figure, 2022), mostly micro-businesses run by women, whose supply chain is fragmented (up to seven channels to buy inputs per salon, Forbes), almost 85% without digital tools, and who lack bank credit: over half of Morado's clients have no bank account and 72% got their first credit from it. Logic: the supplier purchase is a natural place to lend, because the loan is tied to inventory the salon turns over daily, Morado sees the order, the delivery and the repayment behaviour, and alternative data (headcount, location, inventory, appointments) can replace credit scores; starting at about US$820 and raising limits builds a repayment history. Why now: WhatsApp-based commerce and data that lets a lender assess businesses without a credit history. Market size: no independent figure was read. Our estimate: 700,000 salons x an assumed US$6,000 to US$10,000 a year of purchased supplies per salon (our assumption; Forbes says about 20% of a salon's revenue comes from product sales and salons average eight workers) is US$4 billion to US$7 billion of annual supply purchases; if a lender-distributor served 5% to 10% of them at an assumed 10% to 15% gross margin including financing, revenue would be about US$20 million to US$100 million. Morado's own US$12 million of cumulative sales and 28,000 businesses show it is still early. What is different: a Rappi-alumni team with fintech experience applying lending to a niche vertical, a first-credit focus on informal businesses and an inventory-linked loan. Rivals named in the press are SuperBeauty in Colombia and Círculo de Belleza in Mexico (marketplaces). Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does; a Rappi-network founder at pre-seed fits Norte's network-led approach, but no source names Norte in Morado's round; this is our reading. Risks: credit losses on informal micro-businesses and funding cost (the new round includes debt), thin margins in distribution, competition from beauty brands and marketplaces, one-country concentration, and little public data beyond company statements.
note: Facts from https://techcrunch.com/?p=2302919, https://forbes.co/2022/04/20/emprendedores/la-exrappi-que-esta-construyendo-un-amazon-para-peluquerias/, https://latamlist.com/?p=16175, https://moradocolombia.com/sobre-morado. Arithmetic: 700,000 x US$6,000-10,000 = US$4.2bn-7bn; x 5%-10% = US$0.21bn-0.7bn of purchases served; x 10%-15% = US$21m-105m. The per-salon spend, share and margin are our assumptions. Norte lens from https://www.norte.ventures/ read 2026-11-24. Confidence low: no independent market data.

value: Skelt is a Curitiba cosmetics group, known for Brazil's leading self-tanning brand Skelt and for the affordable dermocosmetics brand Creamy, sold online, in its own stores and through pharmacies.
note: Own wording from the company site and Brazil Journal (Mar 2022).

value: Skelt Beauty Brands is a Brazilian beauty group based in Curitiba. It began in 2017, when Gabriel Beleze, then 23 and a long-time fan of self-tanners that were expensive and left skin orange, launched Skelt, a self-tanning product whose formula was developed with a Brazilian pharmaceutical lab and whose first months were financed by his parents. The brand became the reference in autobronzeadores, appeared at the top of independent rankings and was used by celebrities, and it widened into body splash, body makeup, moisturisers and bath products, now with fragrance notes as part of the pitch. In 2019 Beleze and the Curitiba dermatologist Luiz Romancini started Creamy, a dermocosmetics brand with high concentrations of recognised actives at roughly a third of competitors' prices (a 0.3% retinol for R$79 against about R$300 for a multinational brand, said the founder in 2022), made possible by a direct-to-consumer model and lean formulas without fragrance; it launched in November 2019 with R$5 million invested and, by June 2021, had a waiting list of 100,000 people. The business sells online, through its own stores (a target of 55 own stores by the end of 2025) and in pharmacies and cosmetics chains; by March 2022 Skelt was in more than 4,000 points of sale including Raia Drogasil, Drogaria São Paulo and Época Cosméticos, with physical stores making 70% of sales, and Creamy, then sold only digitally, produced almost half of the company's R$56 million revenue in 2021, with a goal of over R$100 million for 2022. Its first outside capital was a R$30 million round from Shift Capital in March 2022 to diversify the portfolio and speed up its skincare pipeline; it also has a third brand, The Joy Lab. In September 2025 it opened its first own factory, in Vinhedo (São Paulo state), which also makes Skelt and The Joy Lab, aiming at 15,000 points of sale by the end of 2025; the same month the group hired Itaú BBA to run the sale of a stake, which the company did not comment on. In November 2025 it reorganised its leadership: Henrique Beleze, who had been COO for five years, became co-CEO alongside Gabriel Beleze. We found no report of a completed sale; Norte lists it as an exit. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, 2026): the group presents itself as Skelt Beauty Brands with several brands, is hiring for CRM, marketing and own retail stores, and runs B2B and B2C fulfilment on a DHL network.

value: Problem: in Brazil the self-tanning and skincare categories were small and expensive (Beleze, 2022): products that left skin orange or cost R$300 for a retinol that could be sold for about R$79, and prescription formulas that patients did not keep buying because of cost. Logic: a digital-first brand that controls formulas (lean, fragrance-free, high-concentration actives) and sells direct can offer a third of the price with healthy margin, build a customer base and community online, and then add pharmacy and own-store distribution; the pandemic accelerated skincare (ABIHPEC reported skincare up 21.9% in 2020, via Forbes). Market size: Brazil's personal care, perfumery and cosmetics market was R$175 billion in 2025, up 6.8% (ABIHPEC with Euromonitor data, O Hoje, 10 Aug 2026), the third largest consumer market of beauty in the world. A skincare and body-care niche share is our estimate: if skincare and body care are about 10% to 15% of the total (our assumption, no page read) the pool is R$17 billion to R$26 billion, and a leading affordable brand at 3% to 5% of it would sell R$0.5 billion to R$1.3 billion a year, compared with Skelt's R$56 million in 2021 and goal of R$100 million for 2022 (the group's growth after 2022 is not documented). What is different: a founder-brand with two distinct hits (the self-tanner category leader and a dermocosmetic price disruptor), a doctor co-founder for credibility, a D2C base with a shift to pharmacy distribution and own stores, and its own factory since 2025. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does; a young consumer-brand founder with proven product-market fit and a follow-on from a specialised growth fund (Shift Capital) matches a connector role; we found no source naming Norte's participation, which our reading cannot assume. Risks: brand-led categories are copied and subject to fashion cycles, retailer and influencer dependence, regulatory and Anvisa risk for dermocosmetics, margin pressure as the mix shifts to pharmacy, and the 2025 sale process suggests the owners were looking for liquidity or a partner.

value: Loopi is a São Paulo fintech that gives medium-sized companies their own platform to offer early payment of supplier invoices (receivables anticipation), with invoice validation, digital assignment and accounting handled by Loopi; it began as a social-commerce app and a crypto on-ramp.
note: Own wording from loopi.finance (read 2026-11-24); the earlier businesses come from Startupi (2021) and InfoMoney (2022).

value: Loopi is a company that has changed its business twice. It was founded in April 2021 in São Paulo by Ricardo Bechara, who had brought Rappi to Brazil in 2017, with Felipe Brasileiro and Cesario Martins, and launched as a "social commerce" app: an endless feed of videos in which content creators show products from partner brands, with a button to buy in a few clicks and delivery; it opened with more than 5,000 products in fashion, beauty and home decoration, and announced a US$5 million first round in June 2021 led by Monashees. In 2022 the team launched LoopiPay, a bridge between Brazil's bank network and decentralised finance: the user pays by Pix and receives crypto tokens straight in a self-custodied wallet such as MetaMask (and can sell the same way), the company charged a fee of 0.9% to 3% plus network gas and, in August 2022, said it offered 1,960 tokens, more than any exchange tracked by CoinMarketCap. By late 2023 it had moved again: Loopi Securitizadora S.A. was incorporated in November 2023 with Bechara as president and Brasileiro as director, and the company, now Loopi Finance, describes itself as an embedded-finance platform for medium-sized companies that want to finance their supply chain. A buyer company gets its own branded platform where its suppliers upload invoices (notas fiscais), the buyer sets the rates, and suppliers anticipate payment in minutes at any time; Loopi provides invoice validation, registration of duplicatas, payment reconciliation, digital signature of the assignment documents, KYC and KYB, and the accounting formalisation. The buyer earns a financial return on a programme it already runs, and the suppliers get better rates and terms than the market. The company calls itself a collective-investment platform and receivables securitiser. We found no press that dates the pivot, names customers or gives traction, and the old crypto site could not be reached.
note: Draws on https://startupi.com.br/startup-que-aposta-em-vendas-pelas-redes-sociais-recebe-aporte-de-us-5-milhoes/ (founded April 2021, social commerce, 5,000 products, US$5M round), https://www.infomoney.com.br/?p=1919465 (LoopiPay launch May 2022, 1,960 tokens, 0.9-3% fee, founders, Rappi Brazil), https://www.projetodraft.com/quer-investir-em-criptomoedas-a-loopipay-ajuda-os-usuarios-a-comprar-e-vender-tokens-de-cripto-via-pix/ (Projeto Draft, 19 Jul 2022: model, 3% fee, investors), https://loopi.finance (current product, CNPJ 53.044.059/0001-48, copyright 2024), the registry https://brasilapi.com.br/api/cnpj/v1/53044059000148 (Loopi Securitizadora S.A. opened 2023-11-29; directors Ricardo Bechara and Felipe Brasileiro) and https://www.cbinsights.com/company/loopi-1/alternatives-competitors (former name LoopiPay). The date of the move to receivables is our estimate (between August 2022 and 2024).

value: Problem: medium-sized companies pay suppliers in 30 to 90 days; their small suppliers need cash earlier and pay high rates to banks and factoring houses, while the buyer has no way to share its better credit with them or to earn from the programme. Logic: a white-label supplier-finance platform lets the buyer offer anticipation at attractive rates funded by investors or funds, with invoice validation and duplicata registration reducing fraud and double-pledging, and the securitiser structure and software make each programme repeatable; the new electronic duplicata (duplicata escritural) regime and registry that the central bank is bringing online make receivables safer to finance. Market size: the Brazilian electronic-duplicata market is estimated to be able to move up to R$12 trillion a year (Capital Aberto, May 2025, citing market estimates); how much is anticipated is not clear from the pages we read. Our estimate for the slice Loopi targets (supplier programmes of medium-sized buyers): if 20,000 medium companies (our assumption) ran programmes anticipating an average of R$20 million of invoices a year (our assumption) that is R$400 billion of volume; at a net fee to the platform of 0.1% to 0.3% of volume (our assumption) it is R$0.4 billion to R$1.2 billion a year, and a company with 1% to 3% of that would earn R$4 million to R$36 million; the figures are illustrative and carry low confidence. What is different: a team that already built consumer products at Rappi scale and pivoted quickly, an embedded-finance model that makes the buyer the distributor, and a securitiser licence structure in house. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and that it brings top funds onto the cap table; Loopi's founders raised US$5 million from Monashees, Canary, OneVC and GFC at first, and a later pivot is the kind of case where a network can help find buyers and funding; this is our reading, not Norte's statement. Risks: two pivots in three years show the original theses did not work, the new model competes with banks, factoring fintechs and the registries' own platforms, credit and fraud losses fall on the investors and the brand, there is no public traction data, and fund-raising from investors for receivables depends on rates and regulatory approval.

value: Elven, legally ElvenWorks Soluções em Tecnologia Ltda., is a Brazilian company built around the idea of reliability for digital products. It started as a consultancy in Cloud, DevOps and SRE (site reliability engineering) and, as companies kept asking it to recommend engineers, created in November 2021 a training programme in SRE for firms and for people changing careers (basic, standard and advanced tracks). Its three founders, Bruno Almeida, Bruno Pereira and Fabrício Lopes, had wide experience in digital products and, seeing few Brazilian firms able to do this work, built the Elven Platform, a B2B SaaS product that watches applications and services actively and manages incidents, including those raised by third-party APMs and open-source tools, in one place. Today the offer has four parts: Elven Observability (metrics, logs and traces, real-time monitors, web monitors and synthetic tests, on an open OpenTelemetry-based stack), Elven Incidentes (alerting, escalation and a mobile app), Elven NOC / Command Center (a 24x7 operations team with an incident commander process) and professional services to implement and tune observability and cloud cost (FinOps). The commercial pitch is explicitly against global tools such as Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace and PagerDuty: billing in reais by use instead of in dollars per host, metric or gigabyte, customer data hosted in Brazil or in the customer's own environment (the company argues for data sovereignty under Brazil's LGPD), support in Portuguese and, it says, costs about 50% lower on average. Named customers include the electronics retailer KaBuM!, the bus-ticket platform Buson, the credit cooperative Unicred (where it replaced weekly crisis rooms with observability by product and a 24x7 command centre), and the AI firm Technium (30% lower cloud cost). In December 2025 Magalu Cloud reported that Elven, which it describes as about six years old and focused on FinOps, SRE, DevOps and observability, had moved the Observability product, its core product and the engine of its growth, from an international cloud to Magalu Cloud after instability and a bill near R$100,000 a month, cutting cost by about 30% and by 40% to 50% on storage, with an environment of more than 30 TB (peaks above 100 TB) and plans to double the infrastructure and grow the customer base by 50% to 70% by year end. The company has added AI agents to its pitch. We found no funding round, investor or revenue figure. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, 2026): CEO Bruno Pereira fronts the company at developer events, it ran its own Observability Day in September 2026, and it is still hiring operations leaders, SREs and NOC analysts.
note: Draws on https://elven.works/sobre.html (founders, 2020, SRE programme November 2021), https://elven.works (products, comparison, cases, 50% savings claim), https://magalu.cloud/blog/case-elven-observabilidade-magalu-cloud/ (Magalu Cloud case, 22 Dec 2025: migration, costs, plans) and https://elven.works/politica-de-privacidade.html (legal name, CNPJ and Barueri seat). Savings and customer outcomes are company-reported. Current state added from LinkedIn posts found by Linked API search-posts on 2026-11-24 (https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:ugcPost:7508212888785002496).

value: Problem: Brazilian companies running critical digital operations pay global observability vendors in dollars, by host, metric or gigabyte, with data hosted abroad and support in English, and many lack the SRE skills to use the tools well (the company's own comparison; the market for SRE, DevOps and Cloud talent is tight, which is why Elven began training engineers). Logic: observability and incident management are mission-critical and recurring, spend grows with cloud usage, and a local vendor that bundles software with an operations team can sell on cost, currency, data residency and responsibility for results; costs of the stack fall when metrics, logs and traces are stored as Parquet in cheap object storage, as Elven did on Magalu Cloud (storage costs 40% to 50% lower than attached disks). Why now: cloud cost pressure (FinOps), the shift to open standards (OpenTelemetry) that reduces lock-in, and AI agents that can act on incidents. Market size: published figures vary widely by scope (search results ranged over an order of magnitude, none of which we could open), and we read only that Brazil held 22.8% of the Latin America, Middle East and Africa IT observability platform market in 2025 (KBV Research), so no dependable Brazilian dollar figure is available. Our bottom-up estimate with labelled assumptions: about 5,000 Brazilian mid-sized and large companies with serious cloud operations, spending R$200,000 to R$500,000 a year on observability, incident and NOC services, is R$1 billion to R$2.5 billion a year; a local leader with 5% to 10% would have R$50 million to R$250 million of revenue, with no public data that Elven is near the lower end. What is different: a combined software-plus-NOC model, pricing in reais, local data, and a team that already trains the market's SRE talent. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and does not meddle with operations; a technical founder team selling to Brazilian CTOs is consistent with a connector role; no source we read names Norte or any investor in Elven, so this is purely our reading. Risks: global vendors can add a Brazilian region and cut price, observability is a crowded and fast-moving category, the business mixes services and software (lower margins), customer concentration, and there is no public information about funding, revenue or customer count.
note: Facts from https://elven.works, https://magalu.cloud/blog/case-elven-observabilidade-magalu-cloud/, https://elven.works/sobre.html; KBV share from https://www.kbvresearch.com/lamea-it-observability-platforms-market/. Arithmetic with our assumptions: 5,000 x R$200k-500k = R$1.0bn-2.5bn; x 5%-10% = R$50m-250m. The number of companies, spend and share are assumptions; the global market figures seen in search results (about US$2.9bn to US$28bn for 2025, depending on scope) came from pages we could not open and are not used. Norte lens from https://www.norte.ventures/ read 2026-11-24. Confidence low.

value: Dr. Jones is a men's grooming and personal-care brand that Guilherme Campos and André Popoutchi founded in 2013, a former banker and a former treasury trader at Itaú BBA, inspired by Dollar Shave Club (sold to Unilever for US$1 billion in 2016) and Harry's. It began inside Beauty Box and sold B2B and through physical retail and marketplaces. In early 2019 it bought the Home Shave Club, a razor-blade subscription club, and at the end of 2019 it made a radical change: it pulled its products from stores and marketplaces and went fully direct-to-consumer, with its own e-commerce and subscriptions. The timing helped, because the pandemic pushed sales online: from March 2020 it grew about 30% a month, cut prices by 15% to 20% in April by passing on the margin saved from retail, and in September 2020 had a run rate of R$7 million and 2,500 subscribers (20% of revenue). Revenue nearly tripled in 2020 to R$3.3 million, reached R$7.3 million in 2021 and the brand closed 2021 with a run rate of R$10 million; the portfolio grew from 11 products in 2020 to 20 products in 2022 (shampoo, face scrub, shaving foam, soaps, an after-shave cream and Abdoburn, an abdominal-fat gel), supported by humorous advertising inspired by Dollar Shave Club that reached almost 5 million views. It had more than 150,000 registered customers and 80,000 active ones in 2022. Funding came from Astella Investimentos, IgniteXL, Igah Ventures and Norte Ventures, plus two founders of Trybe as individuals, and in 2021 and 2022 it tried a bridge round that included an equity crowdfunding offer on Kria (the first for a VC-backed Brazilian startup), which hit its R$3.5 million target with almost 200 backers but was not concluded because of defaults. In October 2022 Grupo Boticário bought 100% in cash for an undisclosed price after a year of talks, giving exit to all the funds, and the founders stayed as executives. Under Boticário, Dr. Jones entered B2B in October 2023 and by July 2024 was in more than 14,000 points of sale, with revenue up 130% in 2023; in 2026 it is listed among the group's brands.

value: Problem: male grooming in Brazil was concentrated in three product types (razors, deodorants, fragrances) held by a few large brands that struggled to innovate (Igah's partner, 2020); razors in particular were sold in stores at high prices and bought in a hurry. Logic: a direct-to-consumer brand with a humorous voice and a subscription for blades (the Dollar Shave Club and Harry's playbook, which ended in a US$1 billion sale to Unilever in 2016) can win customers online, own the relationship and data, and expand into hair, skin and body care with a retention base; in Brazil the pandemic accelerated online buying, and D2C saved the retail margin to cut prices 15% to 20%. Why now (2019 to 2020): digital advertising costs were still low, the founders had already bought a subscription club, and the retail channel was not working for a young brand. Market size: Brazil's men's beauty and personal-care market was about R$22 billion a year in 2020 (Brazil Journal, citing the Igah investor) and about US$5.4 billion in 2022, growing 14.5% a year (Euromonitor, via a Grupo Boticário release); these use different scopes. A bottom-up view of the brand's reachable share: a 1% to 3% share of R$22 billion is R$220 million to R$660 million a year, against the R$10 million run rate at the 2022 exit, so the upside was far above the realised outcome; the founders had also projected R$20 million for 2022 and R$50 million for 2023. What was different: a brand and marketing-led D2C model in a category dominated by established brands; a founder pair from finance (an ex-banker and an ex-trader at Itaú BBA) running a lean operation; subscription revenue (20% of revenue in 2020); and distribution later extended by a strategic buyer. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and brings top funds to cap tables; Norte took part in the 2020 round led by Igah and, per Startups.com.br, suggested crowdfunding for the bridge, and the company was bought by a strategic buyer in 2022 (our reading, not a statement of Norte's reasons). Risks that materialised or remained: small scale at exit, customer-acquisition cost inflation in D2C, the bridge round and crowdfunding that did not close, and dependence on one category (razors) and on marketing spending.

value: AI data company that designs expert-written training tasks, feedback loops and benchmarks for frontier AI labs, using a paid network of remote specialists. It began as the Brazilian student-careers platform Start Carreiras.

Vetto builds data and evaluation systems that help frontier AI labs train and test their models, and it pays experts (doctors, lawyers, engineers, researchers) to create and review the tasks. It does not sell fixed datasets: its pitch is that data is an interface, so it designs learning tasks, expert feedback loops, adaptive benchmarks and evaluation cycles that follow real use. It sells to AI labs (the customer side is a 'get data' enterprise contact, with a product called Atlas) and recruits remote experts through a talent pool at work.vetto.ai, who are paid per task (the expert page shows clinical scenarios at US$50-200 an hour as an example). The company started in 2022 as Start Carreiras, an HR-tech from São José dos Campos founded by three friends from the ITA engineering school, José André Nunes (CEO), Alexandre Bernat and Gabriel Albuquerque, after they found internship hunting poor. It began as software for colleges to onboard students, then became a student-first platform that connects students, companies and universities: by August 2024 it claimed 120,000 students, 500 recruiting companies and 600 institutions, and it shared revenue with universities that distributed its white-label software. In April 2025 it had 700,000 registered students, was adding AI matching and AI interviews (more than 50 hires in the first month of the AI launch) and expected revenue to grow from R$4 million in 2024 to R$25 million in 2025. By January 2026 the company was operating as Vetto, an AI data company: the former Start Carreiras base of students and experts became the supply side, and the business turned to frontier AI labs. In January 2026 Rodrigo Schmidt, an engineering executive with about 15 years at Facebook/Meta, joined as co-founder and CTO, and Lucas Smaira, a former DeepMind researcher, became Head of Research. Its site now publishes research and open benchmarks (Terminal Tasks Open, Vetto Science Bench, Plot Twist Bench, SlopCode Vetted) as proof of its pipelines. Backers named in the press are Maya Capital, Graphene Ventures, Reach Capital and Norte Ventures (seed of R$13 million in April 2025). The public sources do not give Vetto's current revenue, customers or round size after the pivot.

The date of the rename from Start Carreiras to Vetto was not found; the January 2026 article already uses the name. Customer names and current revenue are not public.

value: Problem: frontier AI labs are limited by the quality, not the volume, of their training and evaluation data. Easy web data is largely used up, and improving reasoning, coding and domain skills needs expert-written tasks, careful human feedback and benchmarks that models cannot simply memorise. Labs buy this from a few vendors and are short of skilled people to do the work. Logic and why now: buyers' budgets are large and growing (Sacra estimates Scale AI made about US$2 billion of revenue in 2025, up from US$870 million in 2024, and Meta paid US$14.3 billion for 49% of it), and Meta's stake reportedly pushed other labs, Google among them, to cut ties with Scale and look for neutral suppliers. Vetto's team already had a supply asset: a base of hundreds of thousands of Brazilian students and a way to recruit and pay people at scale. Brazil and Latin America have many qualified professionals (doctors, lawyers, engineers) at lower hourly cost than the US, and Portuguese and Spanish capacity that English-first vendors lack. Market size, a rough order of magnitude: from the vendors we could read, Scale alone was near US$2 billion in 2025, and search summaries of Sacra pages put Surge and Mercor above US$1 billion each, so the expert-data market for labs is plausibly US$5-10 billion a year in 2025-26 (our assumption). If Vetto reached 1% to 3% of it in a good outcome, revenue would be US$50-300 million. What is different: it pairs a research team (ex-DeepMind and ex-Meta leaders) that publishes open benchmarks with a Brazilian expert supply that already runs at scale, and it frames its work as designing the learning experience, not selling labelled rows. value: Digital prescription-drug benefit for companies: employees buy medicines at any pharmacy in Brazil through an app, with AI prescription checks and Pix payment, and employers get a health-management dashboard.

Omni Saúde sells companies a prescription-drug benefit for their employees, the same way an employer buys a meal voucher or a health plan. The employer picks a plan and a monthly balance per person (plans start at about R$50 a month and can exceed R$1,000, with generic-only and any-drug tiers); the employee sends the doctor's prescription in the app, an AI checks it, and the purchase is paid by Pix at any pharmacy in Brazil, with no accredited network (more than 95,000 pharmacies, physical or online). The fiscal receipt is then checked by AI against the prescription. Omni does not earn from selling drugs or from pharmacy commissions: it earns the monthly fee per covered life and makes its margin by managing risk, controlling the claims ratio and preventing fraud, a model Brazil Journal compares with US pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs). A dashboard (Omni Care) shows each employer the use of the benefit, and the company now sells the same infrastructure to insurers and digital health platforms (partnerships with Seguros Unimed and Care Plus). The company was founded in May 2023 by Fernando Domingues, a serial health entrepreneur who co-founded the telemedicine company Conexa Saúde and the medical-cannabis marketplace Cannect Life, and Leopoldo Veras, with more than 25 years in health management. Domingues says the idea follows his telemedicine bet: Brazil's drug coverage inside health plans is small compared with the US. It started with a R$5 million seed in June 2023, had sold more than 15,000 plans by August 2024 (target 50,000 lives and about R$10 million of annual revenue), closed 2024 with R$5 million of revenue, reached about 30,000 lives in May 2025 and, by November 2026, had more than 70 clients, 350,000 paid lives and annualized revenue of R$26 million, aiming at R$30 million by December and R$50 million by the end of 2027. Clients named include Azul, Light, MetLife and Spoleto. Investors named in the press are VEC Investments, Greenrock (the family office of the owners of the Salomão Zoppi laboratory), Norte Ventures, Enseada (the Larragoiti family office, owner of SulAmérica), Wayra (Vivo) and, in the latest round, the venture manager ACNext, plus angels from Neoway, Dr. Consulta and Unimed Nacional. It was picked for KPMG's Emerging Giants programme in 2026, and says AI will be used to predict treatment drop-out and clinical risks.

value: Problem: private health plans in Brazil rarely cover outpatient drugs (the Startups.com.br and Saúde Business pieces point to chronic patients left without cover), so patients and families pay for them from their own pockets. Employers see the cost in absenteeism and in sick leave, and insurers see it in hospital bills when a patient stops treatment. Logic and why now: a drug benefit managed like a voucher (a balance, an app, Pix) is cheap to launch for HR, needs no deals with pharmacy chains, and gives the employer a data dashboard. AI makes the hard part, validating prescriptions and receipts at scale, cheap, and Pix removes card networks. Domingues' own comparison is the US PBM market, which is worth trillions of dollars; Brazil's equivalent is small and still organising. Market size: Brazilian pharmacy retail reached R$241 billion in the twelve months to October 2025 (IQVIA, via Central do Varejo, page read). Prescription drugs for chronic use are a large share of it (our assumption: 40-60%, not sourced). If employers and insurers paid for even 5% of retail drug spend through a benefit like this, that is R$12 billion of annual premiums; at the 5-10% administration and risk margin we assume, revenue would be R$0.6-1.2 billion for the whole category, and a leader holding a third would reach R$200-400 million. Bottom-up check: the company reports R$26 million of annualized revenue from 350,000 lives, or about R$75 a life a year, so each additional million lives is about R$75 million of revenue, a figure we derived from the company's own numbers. What is different: it is a benefit sold to employers and insurers, not a discount card or a pharmacy network; it works at any pharmacy; it earns from risk and fraud control, and its growth is real (revenue from R$5 million in 2024 to a R$26 million run rate in about two years, on the company's own figures). Fit with Norte (our reading): a founder on his third health company, known by Norte's partner Pedro Teo from Conexa and Cannect, where a connector that brings co-investors and enterprise clients helps; Norte entered as a co-investor alongside Greenrock, the follower role its Manifesto describes. Risks: the claims ratio (a bad year of claims or fraud hurts margin), concentration in a few large clients, a possible regulatory reaction from ANS or the drug-price board (CMED) if the product looks like insurance, and large pharmacy chains or health insurers building their own benefit.

Share of chronic-use drugs (40-60%), employer/insurer-paid share (5%) and administration margin (5-10%) are our assumptions: R$241B x 5% = R$12B; x 5-10% = R$0.6-1.2B; one third = R$200-400M. value: Operates online stores and apps for retailers using senior engineers, AI agents and its own software, charging for the results it delivers. Started as the deco.cx website builder for developers.

deco operates online stores for retailers and brands and charges for the results it produces. Its pitch today is that senior engineers, AI agents and its own software run a company's digital experience (site, app, storefront), from audits ranked by revenue to headless storefronts built in weeks, native commerce apps, an AI sales assistant, A/B tests in production, SEO and visibility in AI answers, monitoring around the clock, and integrations with ERP, order management, CRM and payments. Two products sit under that service: the Storefront, with blocks, a site editor and templates, and the Studio, where a company connects its context and builds its own apps and agents. At VTEX Day 2026 (April) deco showed a new CMS that puts the live site next to an AI chat so marketing and design staff can describe a bug or feature and an agent implements it in a preview, a super agent that audits any site across seven dimensions in 10 to 15 minutes, and agents for content and for journey optimisation. It was founded in Rio de Janeiro in 2022 as deco.cx by Guilherme Rodrigues (CEO), Luciano Júnior (CTO) and Rafael Crespo (CMO), three ex-VTEX people (two programmers since their teens and a designer from VTEX's talent team). The first product was a website builder for developers, pitched as an alternative to Wix and WordPress: pick a template, get the code in two minutes, with an own lightweight analytics, A/B testing and hosting, and a marketplace where agencies and freelancers sell programming services. It sold through agencies (36 partner agencies and a Discord with almost 2,500 developers in January 2024). In January 2024 it had 65 signed contracts and 35 sites live, with clients such as Zee.Dog, Embelleze, Osklen and Baw, and aimed at US$1-2.5 million of revenue in the year, with a US self-service launch. Later it moved from selling a tool to operating stores with agents: the company's own pages list case studies (Oficina, New Balance's migration to FastStore in three days) and a May 2026 report says the logistics platform SuperFrete uses deco's AI agents in fraud prevention and customer service. Money raised: about US$600,000 from angels in late 2022, including VTEX founders Geraldo Thomaz and Mariano Gomide, and a US$2.2 million seed in January 2024 led by Maya Capital with FJ Labs, Lanx and Crivo Ventures. value: Problem: large and mid-sized Brazilian retailers run their sites on platforms such as VTEX through agencies. A small fix can wait a week in an agency backlog, and sites decay silently (speed, search visibility, broken funnels). Developers cost a lot and are scarce, and each store needs continuous operation, not a one-time build. Logic and why now: coding agents can now implement a described change inside a preview, and AI answers (search assistants) are a new channel to be visible in. deco came from the platform's inside (its founders worked at VTEX), builds on open-source blocks, and ties its price to results, which lowers the barrier for retailers to try. As agents do more of the engineering, the margin moves from selling developer hours to selling operated outcomes. Market size: ABComm counted R$204.3 billion of e-commerce revenue in Brazil in 2024 and projected R$234.9 billion for 2025 (Mercado&Consumo, read). Our assumption: retailers spend 3-6% of online revenue on technology, agencies and site operation, which would make a R$7-14 billion addressable pool in Brazil in 2025 (R$235B x 3-6%). If deco reached 2-4% of that in a good outcome, revenue would be R$140-560 million; expansion to Latin America and the US (it entered the US in 2024) would multiply it. What is different: it sells operated results rather than seats; it is built by ex-VTEX engineers who know the stack, is open-source at its core, and now ships agents that fix and audit stores. Comparables are the headless CMS and agency model (VTEX FastStore, Shopify partners, Vercel-style platforms), and AI-first agencies. Fit with Norte (our reading): obsessed, technical founders on a second product cycle, backed by Maya and angels from VTEX's founding team; Norte's network of operators from VTEX-like companies and its connector role can bring large retail clients and later-stage funds. Risks: the move from a tool to a service lowers software margins and ties growth to engineers; AI coding assistants may let retailers do this themselves; dependence on the VTEX ecosystem; and few public numbers on revenue after 2024.
