value: Brazilian app for intercity bus travel: it pools travellers to charter executive buses, resells tickets from over 150 bus companies and now owns regulated bus lines.

Buser is a Brazilian app for intercity bus travel that has grown from a group-charter platform into a mix of three businesses: collaborative charter (fretamento colaborativo), regulated bus lines it now owns, and a marketplace that resells tickets from more than 150 bus companies. In the original model, travellers going to the same destination are pooled so that they split the cost of chartering an executive bus from a licensed charter company; Buser sells the seats, runs customer service, pricing, network planning and marketing, and does not own buses or employ drivers (the company's own pitch, and Valor Capital's description), taking a commission from the bus company (reported in 2019 at up to 35%, 20-25% on average). Trips can cost up to about 60% less than a bus-station ticket. Buses carry fatigue cameras and telemetry, and companies and drivers are certified by the transport regulator ANTT. It began when co-founder Marcelo Abritta, from Belo Horizonte, found it cheaper to charter a 48-seat bus for 30 relatives to his wedding in Bahia than to buy 30 tickets (November 2016). With his friend Marcelo Vasconcellos he launched a Facebook page on 2 June 2017, which had 10,000 followers in under 30 days; the first trip, planned for 7 July 2017, was blocked by a court order from incumbents, the passengers were refunded and the press coverage helped. The two founders then raised a seed from Canary, Yellow Ventures and Fundação Estudar Alumni Partners (early 2018), a Series A from Valor Capital, Monashees and Canary (end of 2018) and a Series B led by SoftBank's Latin America fund with Monashees, Valor, Canary and Grupo Globo (October 2019), which carried a plan to spend R$300 million in 12 months. After the pandemic it added a ticket marketplace (end of 2020), parcel delivery inside buses for companies (Buser Encomendas, May 2021), bus financing and urban transport plans, backed by a R$700 million Series C in June 2021 led by LGT Lightrock. It then built a WhatsApp sales channel (expected to reach 35% of revenue in 2022), relaunched its brand in 2024 and, per the press, passed US$100 million of annual revenue in 2024, with 20% growth in operating profit. In 2025 it raised R$30 million in media-for-equity from 4Equity Media Ventures to pay for marketing. In March 2026 it bought two regulated bus companies, Expresso JK and Transportes Santa Maria, its first acquisitions, and in November 2026 co-founder Marcelo Vasconcellos took over as CEO, with Abritta staying on. It reports gross revenue of R$580 million in 2025, expects R$700 million in 2026 and aims for R$1 billion by 2027 through acquisitions of traditional bus companies, AI and the marketplace; it has 14 million registered customers, carries about 5 million passengers a year and wants 6 million in 2027. The company still fights lawsuits from traditional operators and a federal prosecutor over whether its model needs ANTT authorisation, though a Federal Court in Espírito Santo declared the model legal in November 2024.

value: Problem: Brazil moves people by road. Valor Capital counted 4,600 destinations served by buses against 530 by air, and over 300 million bus tickets sold in 2019, twice as many as airline tickets. Yet most routes were run by one company under per-route government authorisations (about 65% of routes with a single operator in 2019), so prices were high and options poor, and many people turned to clandestine transport. Logic and why now: shared chartering lets an asset-light platform pool demand digitally and rent seats on buses that already exist, so a bus fills and costs fall. The model copies the logic of ride-hailing and of Flixbus in Germany, which grew an open market after deregulation (Valor's explanation). Minas Gerais authorising independent charter operators in 2021 and a favourable federal ruling in 2024 moved the regulatory risk in its favour, and Buser now buys licensed bus companies to put its pricing and data into them. Market size: NeoFeed (read, November 2026) cites the regulated road passenger market at R$15-20 billion a year and over 100 million passengers, 60% of which still happens offline. Buser itself reported R$580 million of gross revenue in 2025, so it is already about 3-4% of that market; a strong outcome could be 10-15% (R$2-3 billion), mostly through acquisition and marketplace. The sum is our own: R$15-20B x 10-15% = R$1.5-3B. What is different: it has the brand and the app that millions of Brazilians know, a regulatory track record, and technology (pricing, network planning, fatigue cameras) it can apply to acquired operators; competitors are traditional operators, ClickBus-style marketplaces and BlaBlaCar. Fit with Norte (our reading): this is a Fund I company (Norte's portfolio page), with founders who kept going through years of court battles; as a connector, Norte's role would be introducing top funds (the cap table shows SoftBank, Lightrock, Monashees, Valor) and operators. No source we read says when or in which round Norte invested. Risks: regulation and litigation (ANTT and prosecutors), bus safety incidents and legal responsibility for delays, margin pressure from owning operations, and execution of acquisitions. Travel demand is cyclical, as the pandemic showed.

value: Colombian electricity retailer for businesses that installs a smart meter and gives customers consumption analytics, a single invoice for all their sites and clean-energy options; it is also building distributed solar generation and an energy-software spin-off, Olibia.

Bia sells electricity to businesses in Colombia and wraps it in technology. It buys power in the wholesale market and resells it to companies, installing a smart meter (replacing the traditional one and handling the change of supplier) so the customer can see consumption by site and by hour, get alerts and forecasts, detect reactive-power problems, ask an AI assistant why consumption rose, centralise invoices for many sites in one payment, and see how much of its energy is clean (renewable-energy certificates are available at extra cost). Bia says its tariffs beat the grid operators' average for the same voltage level, and the pitch is that energy should be understood and chosen, not only paid. It was founded in 2022 in Bogotá by two ex-Rappi people, Juan Sebastián Ruales (CEO) and Guillermo Plaza, together with energy-sector executive Leonardo Velásquez. It launched with a US$6 million pre-seed in July 2022 led by Canary, with angels such as the Rappi founders and the founders of NotCo and Frubana. By October 2023, with a Series A of US$16.5 million led by Kaszek, it had more than 1,500 business clients; in November 2024, with a US$8.5 million bridge ahead of a Series B led by RA Capital's Planetary Health fund and IDB Lab, it reported more than 3,000 businesses (Coca-Cola Femsa and Falabella among them), 140 employees and more than US$8 million of monthly revenue, and said it had used up to US$20 million of debt facilities. In August 2026 it raised US$18.5 million led by Kaszek, with Endeavor Catalyst, RA Capital and the IDB, bringing total capital to about US$40 million, and reorganised as a group with three units: energy retail (more than 4,000 companies, including Coca-Cola, Falabella, Ikea and Parmalat, about 50 GWh a month, or roughly 0.7% of the national market), distributed generation (small hydro plants and 'remote panel' solar communities of 1 MW, aiming for at least 15 communities in 2026) and Olibia, a software spin-off of the operating system Bia built for its own acquisition, billing, collections and trading, in talks with customers in five countries and aimed at gas, water and telecoms as well as power. The CEO says the business will grow 60-70% in 2026 with 92% retention in the first cohort and an NPS of 83, and that it will open a free market-intelligence platform to the whole industry. Backers named in the press include Kaszek, Canary, Nazca, 8VC, Global Founders Capital, EWA Capital, WildSur, RA Capital, IDB Lab and Endeavor Catalyst; Norte Ventures appears in aggregator investor lists and in a 2026 LinkedIn event post that tags it, but no round article names it.

value: Problem: Colombian businesses buy electricity without seeing what they use until the bill arrives, with limited choice of supplier, and tariffs rose 15.3% a year between 2021 and 2024 (Corficolombiana, cited by Forbes Colombia), the sharpest rise in 23 years after a drought. A regulated or contract customer with several sites has no clean data, no forecast and no single invoice. Logic and why now: the market for larger customers is open to competition, so a retailer that buys well in the wholesale market (using hydrology and weather models) and installs its own smart meter can give a lower price and data at the same time. The meter and billing data are also a software asset, which Bia now spins off as Olibia. Rising prices and El Niño make customers receptive. Market size: Bia says 50 GWh a month is about 0.7% of the Colombian market (Ecosistema Startup, read), implying about 7,100 GWh a month or about 86 TWh a year nationally (our arithmetic: 50 / 0.007). At an assumed average of US$0.10-0.15 per kWh, that is about US$8-13 billion a year of electricity sales in Colombia; the part open to Bia's customers (businesses above the regulated threshold) is only a share of it (our assumption: 20-30%, so US$2-4 billion). Bia's own revenue run-rate of more than US$8 million a month (about US$100 million a year) is therefore roughly 2.5-5% of that addressable part, and a leader at 15-20% would be US$300-800 million, before Latin American expansion and software. What is different: the company combines a retail licence with its own meter, billing and trading software and reports 92% retention and an NPS of 83, which is uncommon for an energy supplier. A comparable the company itself names is Kraken Technologies, spun out of Octopus Energy, which in September 2025 reported US$500 million of contracted annualised revenue and more than 70 million accounts (Ecosistema Startup) - Bia's software unit is much earlier, with no licence revenue reported yet. Fit with Norte (our reading): ex-Rappi founders, a network of Latin American operators, and a cap table with Kaszek, Canary and Nazca fits Norte's co-investor role; the Manifesto says it brings top funds and operators into cap tables. No article says what Norte put in or when. Risks: wholesale-price exposure in a drought year (the CEO says demand is matched with contracts), regulatory change in Colombia's electricity market, financing needs for the energy contracts and solar communities (debt, guarantees), and the distraction of three business lines.

value: Brazilian fintech that gives manufacturers a co-branded Pix virtual card and an AI credit assistant so their small retail customers can buy in instalments while the manufacturer is paid upfront and Robbin carries the risk.

Robbin is a Brazilian fintech that lets manufacturers and distributors sell on credit to their small retail customers without carrying the credit risk. A large industry offers its retailers a co-branded virtual card (it sits in a digital wallet app and runs on Pix instead of the Visa or Mastercard networks); the retailer buys in instalments from the industry's suppliers and earns points (convertible into discounts on future purchases or Livelo points), and the industry receives the money upfront while Robbin takes over the collection. Robbin builds and runs the whole credit journey: customer onboarding with automatic validation and fraud detection, credit intelligence and limits, risk management and capital. Its AI sales assistant, Robbinson, runs on WhatsApp, the channel the sales team already uses, and approves credit in real time during the sales conversation (the site claims decisions in 30 seconds instead of two weeks, and that a network buys 73% more; these are company claims). It sells to textile, construction materials, electronics, auto parts, food, pharma, household goods, telecom and marketplace players, and also offers its AI agents (KYC and anti-money-laundering checks in about 20 seconds, credit, monitoring and collection) to banks, insurers and asset managers. It was founded in 2023 (about two and a half years before May 2026) by Leonardo Moura (CEO; about 15 years at XP, where he built the international debt-capital-markets franchise, and at Itaú BBA in London and New York), Henrique Meyer (COO; Itaú BBA, Citi and HSBC debt markets) and Tomás Corrêa (CTO; co-founder and CTO of OpenCo, the digital lender formed by the merger of Geru and Rebel with SoftBank backing, where he led technology for almost ten years). The founders' thesis is that retailers got modern card and instalment experiences while the link between industry and retail was left with short, rigid terms and badly calibrated limits. In May 2026 it announced its first institutional round, a US$8 million seed co-led by Canary, Atlântico and Caravela, with AB Seed, Norte Ventures, Clocktower and Tomorrow Capital, plus a US$100 million receivables fund (FIDC) structured with Augme, the XP manager, to fund the credit it extends (it plans to deploy all of it by the end of 2027). Until then its funding was bilateral lines from banks, which had financed about R$200 million of credit since inception. It had eight partner industries (Cantu Pneus, Chilli Beans, Baterias Moura, Malwee, Brinox, Votorantim, Tigre and Gerdau's Juntos Somos Mais marketplace among them), a potential base of more than 300,000 small and mid-sized businesses linked to them, a target of 50 industries by the end of 2026, and a default rate it says is below the 5.5% Brazilian-central-bank SME average. It targets industries with annual revenue above R$500 million.

value: Problem: a manufacturer selling to thousands of small retailers has to decide, for each one, whether to give credit, how much and for how long. Short, rigid terms and badly calibrated limits cap its sales, and the retailer has no access to the instalment and benefits experience a consumer gets. Banks serve these small companies badly, and the industry carries the credit risk and the collection effort on its balance sheet. Logic and why now: Pix gives a cheap real-time payment rail, so a card-like product does not need card networks; AI agents make onboarding, fraud checks, limit setting and collection cheap enough for small tickets; and a receivables fund (FIDC) lets the company fund credit without using its own equity. The industry gets cash upfront, the retailer gets terms, and Robbin earns on the transaction and the credit spread. Market size: no published figure for B2B trade credit in Brazil was found (search results gave only default statistics). Our bottom-up estimate: the company says its eight partner industries give access to more than 300,000 small and mid-sized businesses. If each bought R$50-150 thousand a year on instalment terms (our assumption), that is R$15-45 billion of annual purchases from only the current partners; at an assumed 2-4% revenue per real financed (fees and credit spread), the revenue pool is R$0.3-1.8 billion a year from them alone. With 50 industries (the company's end-2026 goal) the pool could be several times that. A strong outcome of, say, 10-20% of such a pool would be several hundred million reais of revenue. What is different: it combines a co-branded Pix card owned by each industry, AI agents in WhatsApp and a fund that carries the risk, run by founders from debt capital markets and from a digital lender. Comparables (SME trade-credit fintechs and card issuers) were not researched. Fit with Norte (our reading): obsessed, experienced founders at the earliest institutional stage, with credit and technology experience, which matches a follower role in a seed led by Canary, Atlântico and Caravela; Norte's network of operators and industry executives can open doors to large manufacturers, the customers the model depends on. Risks: credit losses and funding cost if the portfolio grows faster than risk models learn (a thin loss history, a young company); dependence on a few large industries; competition from banks and trade-credit fintechs; and the need for repeated FIDC capacity.
note: No published market size for B2B trade credit in Brazil was found (a search returned only Serasa blog and Forbes default statistics, not used). Our bottom-up: 300,000 linked SMEs (company claim, Finsiders) x R$50-150k yearly purchases (assumption) = R$15-45B; x 2-4% revenue yield (assumption) = R$0.3-1.8B. value: Brazilian technology-skills school that began as an income-share developer bootcamp and now sells AI courses, workshops and corporate training, including a programme for lawyers with OAB state sections.

Trybe is a Brazilian school for technology skills that began by training software developers and is now centred on teaching artificial intelligence at work. In its first form, a developer course of about 12 months (later also mobile, data science, cybersecurity and data engineering) could be paid only after the graduate got a job above a salary floor: the student paid up to 17% of the salary, over up to five years, for a total of R$36,000 (the company calls it the shared-success model, MSC; the press calls it an income share agreement, ISA). Trybe made money from those instalments and from deals with employers who hired graduates; 94% of graduates were working within 30 days of graduating (company claim, 2021). It built a financing arm, Trybe SCD, authorised by the Central Bank as a direct credit company in May 2021, and raised a R$50 million receivables fund (FIDC) in March 2021 to fund the ISA. It was founded in August 2019 by five partners who earlier built AppProva, an education-data startup with 5 million students that was sold to Somos Educação: Matheus Goyas (CEO), Cláudio Lensing, João Daniel Duarte, Marcos Moura and Rafael Torres. Six months after opening it raised a R$42 million Series A led by Atlantico (about US$10 million), with Norte among the investors, then a US$6 million extension led by Base Partners in January 2021, the acquisition of the Santa Catarina software house Jungle Devs in June 2021 and a R$145 million (US$27 million) Series B in October 2021 led by Base Partners and Untitled, at a valuation of about R$1.3 billion. By then it had 2,200 students, 130 partner companies (CI&T, Ford, Localiza, Méliuz, Thoughtworks, XP), more than 190,000 applications and students in eight countries besides Brazil. When tech hiring turned in 2022, Trybe cut 47 people (about 10% of nearly 500) in August 2022 and 128 people (about 35% of staff) in June 2023, saying it aimed at breakeven within 180 days; it launched an intensive live course (FIT) and a free JavaScript course for 2,000 people to bring in students. Its public site today sells AI courses, workshops and training for companies and for lawyers: it says more than 1,000 companies have developed their teams with it, that it is the AI-training partner of 16 OAB state sections, and that its AI-literacy programme for law, run with the OAB sections, Jusbrasil and ITS Rio, has had more than 100,000 professionals. The date of the move to AI training is not given in the sources read; no round after 2021 was found.

value: Problem: Brazil's tech sector cannot find enough trained people: Brasscom projected demand of 797,000 professionals from 2021 to 2025 against 53,000 graduates a year in technology courses, a gap of 106,000 a year (Convergência Digital, December 2021). Many candidates cannot pay for a bootcamp up front. Now a second gap has opened, in using AI at work: employees and professional groups such as lawyers need practical training at speed, because the tools change weekly. Logic and why now: the income-share model aligns the school with the student's job outcome and made it attractive to investors in 2020-21, when hiring was strong; the 2022-23 downturn showed its weakness (graduates take longer to place, financing needs are large). The new AI-training line moves to a lighter model (subscriptions, workshops, corporate training) that sells to employers and professional associations with a distribution channel, the OAB, and does not carry student credit. Market size: we found no published figure for the market of corporate AI training in Brazil. Our bottom-up estimate for lawyers: Brazil has on the order of one million registered lawyers (our assumption, not read), so an annual subscription of R$1,000-2,000 (assumption) would give a pool of R$1-2 billion; a 5-10% share is R$50-200 million. For company training, the company says it has served over 1,000 companies; at R$30,000-100,000 per contract (assumption) and 300-500 contracts a year, revenue would be R$10-50 million. These are our assumptions only. What is different: it has a large Brazilian base of developers' alumni and employer relationships, a brand known by 190,000 applicants, and an association channel (OAB) that lowers the cost of acquiring customers; it also has experience of running credit for students. Fit with Norte (our reading): Norte invested at the Series A when the founders were second-time entrepreneurs with a sold company (AppProva) and a clear talent-supply problem; Norte's network of operators who hire developers fits the early distribution need. Risks: the 2023 layoffs show a dependence on tech hiring; the AI-training market is crowded (universities, platforms, vendors) and low-priced; the pivot is recent and little is published on its revenue; the finance arm's loan book from 2020-22 may still weigh on results.

value: Brazilian payment orchestrator for physical stores: one integration connects a shop's point-of-sale software to every acquirer and Pix provider and routes each transaction by lowest cost.

Destaxa is a Brazilian payments company that sits between a shop's point-of-sale (PDV) software and the card machines and payment processors, so one integration lets a retailer use any acquirer or Pix provider and route each transaction through the cheapest option. It describes itself as the first payment orchestrator for physical (offline) merchants and says it will never be a payment processor, only infrastructure, which keeps it neutral between acquirers. Its customers are the software houses and commercial-automation vendors that build PDV systems (it was connected to about 130 of them in 2024, with nearly 150,000 PDV clients, of which fewer than 5,000 were Destaxa's), and through them the merchants, with monthly revenue of R$100,000 to R$1 million. Products on its site: a TEF (card-payment integration) and an advanced version, the DTX+ web platform to set parameters for every client in real time, a card-and-Pix integration for Android smart terminals (it bets on the 'androidisation' of the PDV market, where each acquirer's Android machine forces vendors to maintain a separate integration), an 'Oferta Inteligente' programme that lets automation vendors earn a share of their clients' card transactions, receivables advance (the cheapest working capital a merchant has) and a partnership to sell energy directly from the producer with savings of up to 30%. Earlier it sold a merchant-side dashboard with reconciliation of cards and banks, fee audits and cash-flow automation. It was founded in 2021 by Felipe Ayres, a third-time entrepreneur (he earlier created the asset manager F3 Capital and the sub-acquirer Nexu), together with businessman Sigvard Von Baranow Neto. Ayres got the idea of orchestration after a trip to India to study UPI, where he met a former sub-acquirer who had moved to orchestration. Growth in new clients per month went from 5-20 in 2022 to 50-100 in 2023 and 300-500 in 2024, with a target of 5,000 a month by mid-2025. Processing reached more than R$2 billion a year at the end of 2023 and about R$4 billion a year in mid-2024; in June 2024 it was testing its platform as infrastructure for acquirers (one in test, one in talks). Backers named in the press are Quona Capital (lead of the 2022 seed), Caravela, Norte Ventures, the angels Tiago Dalvi (Olist) and Alessio Alionço (Pipefy), and, in the November 2023 R$30 million round, Astella (lead), Supera, Quona, Caravela and Endeavor ScaleUp Ventures. The CEO said in June 2024 that a Series A was planned for early 2025; the sources read do not show that it happened, and no later news was found.

value: Problem: a small merchant sells with many card machines and contracts, does not know which acquirer is cheapest for each transaction, and cannot easily renegotiate. The software house that makes its point-of-sale system must build and maintain a separate integration for each acquirer, a growing burden as Android terminals multiply. Logic and why now: Pix and the open card market gave merchants choice, and Android machines made it possible to run one payment app on any acquirer's terminal. An orchestrator that is neutral and cheap to integrate can give the software house new revenue (a share of each transaction) and the merchant the lowest-cost route per transaction. Market size: Abecs reports R$4.5 trillion of card volume in Brazil in 2025 (Finsiders, read), with online purchases above R$1 trillion, leaving roughly R$3.4 trillion in physical stores (our subtraction: 4.5 - 1.0 and a little). Destaxa processes about R$4 billion a year (2024, company), about 0.1% of the in-store volume. If it reached 5% of in-store volume (about R$170 billion) and kept a net take of 0.05-0.15% of volume (our assumption: a fraction of the spread it helps save, shared with the PDV vendor), revenue would be R$85-255 million. A strong outcome is therefore in the low hundreds of millions of reais of revenue. What is different: neutrality (never a processor), integration with about 130 PDV vendors (distribution, not direct sales), and a revenue share for the vendor. Online orchestrators (Yuno, Malga, PoolPay) and the offline player Shipay are named as comparables by Finsiders. Fit with Norte (our reading): a serial founder with a payments background and an infrastructure-style product, at the seed stage with Quona and Caravela leading; Norte joined as follower in 2022 and can help with introductions to PDV vendors, acquirers and later funds. Risks: acquirers may cut costs for vendors directly or build their own multi-acquirer terminals; low take rate per transaction; concentration in the PDV vendors' channel; and no published sign of growth or a Series A since mid-2024.
